title: The Lantern Race
summary: In a mountain village, Mila and Teo, friends and rivals, carry their paper lanterns up the path. Tonight, the race is going to change its rules.

scenes.text:
High up on the mountain, where the clouds sit down to rest on the rooftops, there was a little village called Alto Sereno.

Once a year, the village children made paper lanterns and carried them up the stony path to Lookout Rock.

It wasn't a race for running. It was a race for taking care. The winner was the lantern that reached the top still alight.

Mila and Teo were neighbours. Friends all their lives, and rivals all their lives.

Last year, she had won. The year before, he had.

"This year I'm going to win," said Mila, her fringe all messy.

"We'll see about that," said Teo.

And they both laughed without meaning to.

That afternoon, each of them went off to find their materials.

Mila went into the woods for willow twigs, the thinnest ones, the ones that bend without breaking. She stepped on the leaves on purpose, to hear them crunch.

Teo went down to the river to cut canes, and on the way he found three flat stones for his collection.

They met again on the path, each of them hugging a bundle of sticks.

"Are you making a square one again?" asked Mila.

"I'm making a better one than yours," said Teo.

They walked back to the village side by side, without saying anything. That's how friends who are also rivals walk.

"Tomorrow," she said at her door.

"Tomorrow," he said.

Mila's kitchen smelled of cinnamon.

Grandma took some very thin tissue paper out of the cupboard, as blue as the night sky. Mila tied the willow twigs together, one by one, until they made a round basket, so light it almost floated. Then she glued on the paper carefully, with her tongue between her teeth, and painted a little star on each side.

"It's going to fly beautifully," said Grandma.

"It's going to get there first," said Mila.

Just then, from the other side of the wall, in the house next door, came a little tapping.

It was Teo, working.

Mila pressed her ear to the wall, held her breath and smiled without meaning to.

On the other side of that same wall, Teo was working in the barn, with a torch hanging from a nail.

His lantern wasn't going to be round. It was going to be a six-pointed star, with the canes crossed like the spokes of a wheel.

It took him three tries. On the second one, a cane snapped: crack!

Teo had to start again, huffing through his nose so as not to get cross.

"Slowly gets you there sooner," said his dad, passing him the glue.

Teo covered the star with orange paper, the colour of tangerines, and painted an eye on every point, so the lantern could see the way.

And he thought, without saying it out loud, that Mila's eyes were going to go very wide when she saw it.

The next evening, the square looked like a treasure chest full of lights. There were red lanterns, green ones, golden ones and stripy ones. It smelled of thick hot chocolate and toasted corn.

Don Nicolás, the baker, climbed onto the edge of the fountain.

"You go up the path to Lookout Rock," he said. "The winner is the lantern that arrives still lit. And nobody blows out their neighbour's!"

Everyone laughed.

Mila and Teo stood side by side, as always. Not looking at each other, and looking at each other.

"Nice star," said Mila, very quietly.

"Nice basket," said Teo.

And at that moment, from the church tower, rang the bell.

The children left the village like a river of lights.

At first everyone wanted to run. But they soon learned the lesson: if you run, the flame goes out. And the river of lights became slow, careful, beautiful.

Mila carried her blue basket at chest height, with both hands. Teo carried his orange star high on a stick, like a flag.

The path climbed between dark pine trees. Down below, the village grew smaller and smaller, with its yellow windows.

Mila was already imagining her name on the sign in the bakery. Teo was imagining his.

And they were both so busy imagining that they didn't notice the mountain beginning to take a deep breath.

And then it came.

From the summit, whistling through the branches, down swept a gust.

It caught Teo's star by one point. The paper puffed up, stretched… and tore. The candle went out in one breath.

The stick slipped out of his hands and fell onto the path.

Teo stood still, with empty hands.

The other children went past him, with their lights, without stopping. Teo thought about the three tries. About the eyes he had painted, one by one. About his dad saying: slowly gets you there sooner.

All of that, lying there, broken on the ground.

He clenched his teeth so the tears wouldn't come. Further up, Mila's blue light had almost reached Lookout Rock.

Mila noticed before she saw: she couldn't hear Teo behind her any more.

She turned round. Down below, at the bend in the path, there was a boy standing still beside a broken star.

Mila looked at Lookout Rock, so close that she could already see people's faces. She looked at her blue lantern, alight and perfect.

She stood still. She breathed in deeply.

And she went back down.

"It broke," said Teo, without looking up.

"I saw," said Mila. And she held her blue basket right between the two of them. "Take the other side."

"What about your race?"

"It's our race."

Teo slowly lifted his hand, still not quite believing it, and took hold of the edge of the basket. And the light, which until then had shone on one face, began to shine on two.

They climbed the last stretch together, with four hands around a single light.

They had to walk in step, which made them stumble, and laugh, and in the end walk like one person with two heads.

When they reached Lookout Rock, the whole village was watching them.

There was a short silence. And then, a round of applause that echoed across the whole mountain.

Don Nicolás scratched his head under his cap.

"Well," he said. "One lantern wins here. And this lantern has two owners."

He cut his champion's ribbon in two, and hung a piece round each of their necks.

Down below, the village shone. Up above, the stars shone. And in between, a blue tissue-paper basket, still alight.

They walked back to the village slowly, because nobody was in a hurry any more.

In Grandma's kitchen they drank hot chocolate from cups with flowers painted on them. Teo left his broken star on the table, with its points all bent.

"We'll fix it tomorrow," said Mila, her eyes heavy. "And next year we'll make an enormous one, together."

"One that doesn't break," yawned Teo.

Then each of them went to bed, on either side of the same wall.

Mila snuggled under her blankets. And before she fell asleep, she knocked softly on the wall with her knuckles.

On the other side, after a moment, someone answered the same way.

Goodnight, they meant. And also: we won.
